results.key_findings: RRMS accounts for approximately 85% of MS cases at onset. output.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria require demonstration of dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) for an MS diagnosis. DIS is met by T2 lesions in at least 2 of 4 characteristic locations (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal cord). DIT is demonstrated by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI, a new T2 or gadolinium-enhancing lesion on follow-up imaging, or — importantly under the 2017 revision — by the presence of CSF-specific oligoclonal bands. Choice of DMT should balance efficacy, safety profile, and patient factors including reproductive plans and comorbidities.

results.authors: Wingerchuk DM, Banwell B, Bennett JL, et al.
results.key_findings: NMOSD core clinical criteria include optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome (nausea/hiccups), brainstem syndrome, diencephalic syndrome, and cerebral syndrome. AQP4-IgG seropositive NMOSD requires one core clinical feature. Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (spanning ≥3 vertebral segments) is a hallmark MRI finding. Short-segment cord lesions (<3 segments) and periventricular Dawson fingers are more consistent with MS.
results.title: International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders

results.key_findings: MOGAD is characterised by MOG-IgG positivity by cell-based assay, with core presentations including optic neuritis (often bilateral), myelitis, ADEM-like phenotype, and cortical encephalitis. Cerebellar involvement can occur. MRI lesions in MOGAD often partially or fully resolve, unlike MS. Thalamic and cortical lesions favour MOGAD over MS.
results.title: Diagnosis of MOG antibody-associated disease: International MOGAD Panel proposed criteria

output.summary: NMOSD is distinguished from MS by AQP4-IgG seropositivity, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, area postrema involvement, and the absence of classic periventricular Dawson fingers on MRI. MOGAD requires MOG-IgG positivity by cell-based assay and typically presents with optic neuritis, myelitis, or ADEM-like syndromes; lesions often show more complete resolution than MS. Both require exclusion (negative AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG by cell-based assay) before a confident MS diagnosis. Short-segment spinal cord lesions, periventricular lesions in Dawson fingers configuration, and CSF oligoclonal bands in the absence of AQP4-IgG or MOG-IgG support MS.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Reyes is a 32-year-old right-handed Hispanic woman, a school teacher, who presents to the emergency department with an 8-day history of progressive left arm numbness and worsening gait unsteadiness. Eight days ago she noticed tingling and numbness in her left arm, starting at the shoulder and spreading distally to the hand over 2-3 days. She describes the sensation as persistent pins and needles, worst over the dorsum of the left hand and forearm, non-positional, unrelated to neck position at the time of onset. Over the same period she began to notice difficulty with left-hand fine motor tasks: fumbling when buttoning her daughter's clothing and dropping objects she was holding. Concurrently, her gait has become progressively unsteady. She reports feeling like she is walking on a boat, with a tendency to veer to the left, and she has had to widen her stance to avoid falling. She tripped twice on flat ground over the past 3 days. This morning she noticed that neck flexion causes an electric shock-like sensation that shoots into her left arm and left leg, prompting her husband to bring her to the emergency department. On further questioning, she reports that approximately 11 months ago she developed tingling and numbness in the left arm lasting about 3 weeks, which was attributed by her primary care physician to a pinched nerve in her neck; no imaging was performed and the episode resolved spontaneously. She also describes unexplained fatigue disproportionate to her activity level for the past 6-8 months, and she noticed that her walking became noticeably worse after jogging or after a hot shower during the current episode. She denies visual loss, eye pain, diplopia, facial numbness, difficulty swallowing, hearing changes, bladder or bowel incontinence, fever, weight loss, joint pain, skin rashes, oral ulcers, dry eyes, or dry mouth. She has no history of seizures or head trauma. There is no family history of neurological disease.
